chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

There was a woman from Thaqif under his guardianship, and from her he had a son named Ibrahim. A slave girl of Thaqif came to her and said to her, 'Who is this husband of yours?' She said, 'Muhammad ibn Ali.' She said, 'Because of that, there are companions in Kufa, a people who insult the Salaf (early generations) and they say...'

He said, 'So he freed her way (divorced her).' He said, 'I saw him after that, and it had become apparent upon him, and something had eroded from his body.' He said, 'So I said to him, 'The separation from her has become apparent upon you.' He said, 'And you have seen that?' I said, 'Yes.'

key_terms.السَّلَف: The Salaf, referring to the early generations of Muslims

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Abu Ja'far divorce the woman from Thaqif?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the principle of *al-wala' wa al-barra'* (alliance and disavowal) by linking marital compatibility to religious factionalism, specifically the Thaqifis' hostility toward the Salaf. Imam Abu Ja'far (AS) divorced his Thaqifi wife not merely for tribal origin, but due to their specific political-religious alignment, demonstrating that social ties can impact spiritual standing. The visible physical decline of the Imam underscores the profound spiritual weight of separating from those associated with opposing factions.
